transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Marcus Li (Redwood SRE), Evan Morales (CTO, Evergreen Analytics), Emily Tran (Lead ML Eng), Samir Patel (Infra)
Shared artifacts: 128k-long-context-deep-dive deck (link), perf-benchmarks-128k.csv (link), VPC-onprem-checklist.docx (link)

Summary: deep technical dive focused on long-context serving (>=128k tokens) — chunking strategies, KV cache behavior under extreme context, batching tradeoffs, quantization effects on memory and perf, and VPC/on-prem operational constraints. Customer wants predictable latency for retrieval-augmented generation over multi-document corpora with 128k+ active context and strong audit/compliance needs.

[00:00] Alex: ok hi everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick intro—i'm Alex, AE at Redwood, and with me is Priya our SE. Marcus is here for SRE/ops questions. can we do quick intros?
[00:14] Evan: yeah Evan here, CTO at Evergreen. Emily is our lead ML eng, Samir handles infra. we're looking to evaluate long context serving, 128k plus, for our research search app.
[00:30] Priya: great, high level we'll cover architecture, kernel/attention optimizations (flashattention etc), kv cache management, chunking and recombine strategies, and then ops (VPC, on prem). we'll also call out quantization options and tradeoffs.
[00:48] Emily: perfect, we have a couple constraints — must keep 95th latency under 500ms for incremental completion tokens when reading from a 128k active context. throughput also matters, we expect ~20 concurrent sessions at peak.
[01:05] Samir: security is critical — SOC2, KMS for keys, audit logs, and we need private control plane or VPC peering.
[01:18] Priya: noted. quick question on your workload: are you streaming the whole 128k into the model every request, or doing an RAG-style chunk+retrieve prior to generation?
[01:32] Evan: RAG-style, but we sometimes need the model to attend across many retrieved chunks — like summarizing across dozens of docs that together exceed 128k. so we want the model to see a coherent logical context.
[01:45] Alex: okay that maps to what we've seen — two high level approaches: 1) pursue a single large-context model that accepts 128k natively, or 2) chunk + recombine where you feed the model overlapping windows and stitch results, possibly with a KV cache to avoid recomputing prefixes.
[02:08] Priya: right. for native 128k models there's heavy memory pressure — KV cache alone becomes huge (per token KV state). quantization (int8 or 4-bit) helps reduce memory but can affect output quality; we typically recommend mixed strategy.
[02:28] Emily: when you say KV cache becomes huge, can you quantify?
[02:33] Priya: yes, rough numbers: for a 7B-ish transformer, full float16 KV per token can be about 1.5KB/token; at 128k that's ~192MB of KV per request; for larger models it's multiple GB. with quantization to int8 we've seen ~2-2.5x memory reduction. so on a shared GPU that matters.
[02:55] Samir: so for our 20 concurrent sessions that's ... math in my head is scary.
[03:01] Marcus: yeah, that's why we do batching and sharing of KV cache across similar prefixes where possible. Redwood's runtime supports prefix cache reuse and pinned caches for sessions in Dedicated.
[03:18] Evan: how deterministic is prefix reuse? our users will have slightly different retrieval sets per session.
[03:25] Priya: it's heuristic — we key the cache by exact prefix fingerprints; similar prefixes won't automatically dedupe unless you canonicalize text at retrieval time. also we have feature flags for chunk dedupe and partial-match reuse. there's a tradeoff between cache hit rate and complexity of canonicalization.
[03:43] Emily: tell us about attention optimizations — flashattention and any recompute tricks that help 128k.
[03:50] Priya: flashattention reduces memory by streaming attention computation and avoiding large intermediate matrices, it helps a lot for long sequences. we also use windowed attention for extremely long inputs — e.g., sparse attention patterns or sliding-window + global tokens. ALiBi or rotary embeddings are supported; some models with RoPE can be more expensive for very long extrapolations but we have kernel-level optimizations.
[04:14] Evan: are positional encodings the limiting factor for 128k?
[04:18] Priya: sometimes — RoPE scales but you need careful handling for extrapolation; we recommend models with linearized attention variants or explicit long-context optimizations. we also use chunked attention where you compute cross-chunk attention via summary tokens to avoid O(N^2) blowup.
[04:35] Alex: note — there are approximate attention methods (block-sparse, Linformer-ish) but quality varies. if you need full cross-document coherence, chunking+stitching with a robust recombine prompt often gives pragmatic results.
[04:50] [05:00] Speaker 4 (customer, mislabelled): so how does Redwood handle cache eviction? what if session length grows beyond available KV memory?
[05:08] Marcus: good Q. we have LRU-style eviction for session caches and we can spill to host memory when configured on Dedicated/Private. spilling adds latency; we can also pin hot sessions to reserved GPUs. we expose metrics for cache hit/miss and eviction rates in Console.
[05:28] Emily: spill to host is acceptable as long as tail latency is bounded.
[05:33] Priya: yes, this is where mixing quantization and batching helps — by reducing per-token state we reduce spills. also incremental generation with local chunk recomputation for recent segments is often faster than full spill+reload.
[05:49] Evan: walk us through a recommended architecture for our use-case.
[05:52] Priya: recommended path: Dedicated capacity in a VPC with pinned GPU pools; use an optimized 128k-capable model if you can accept some model calibration, otherwise do chunked RAG with a KV cache pinned per-session and sliding-window recompute for older segments. use int8 quantization profile for KV to reduce memory, and keep float16 for compute where needed.
[06:15] Alex: and for failover, route to a lower-context variant for burst traffic automatically — Redwood's smart routing can fallback to a 32k or 16k variant with a note to the app that it's degraded.
[06:29] Samir: are there any known issues with quantized KV caches and correctness? we've seen hallucination increases in some internal tests.
[06:38] Priya: possible. quantization can slightly change logits; we recommend running a small eval suite. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles per model and workload and we can tie regression alerts to your eval prompts. we'll help run AB tests.
[06:55] Emily: what's the expected throughput tradeoff — latency per token vs batch size when you're doing continuous batching on 128k contexts?
[07:05] Marcus: continuous batching groups requests to improve utilization but increases per-request latency variability. with large KV caches, batching helps amortize KV load across similar prefixes. For your SLO (95th < 500ms), you may need a lower batching timeout (e.g., 5-10ms) and more dedicated capacity.
[07:27] Priya: also consider prefix caching at the region edge for repeated retrievals; if retrievals are similar across sessions we see big wins.
[07:36] Evan: about on-prem — can we run Redwood Private in our air-gapped environment?
[07:41] Alex: yes, Redwood Private supports an on-prem bundle plus private control plane options. for strict air-gap we ship an installable package; some telemetry features are optional. KMS/HSM integrations are available for key isolation.
[07:55] Samir: what about model updates and kernel selection when we're on-prem?
[07:59] Priya: kernel selector runs locally; we ship a recommended image with kernel heuristics. you can pin to specific kernel sets. model updates can be staged via a canary cluster in your environment.
[08:12] Emily: there's often confusion around "KV cash" in our notes—ha — is that a term?
[08:16] Alex: (laughs) kv cache, kv cash, same thing in speech.
[08:20] [08:30] Evan: question on chunking: do you recommend overlapping windows or distinct splits and then a final recombine pass?
[08:36] Priya: overlapping windows reduce boundary effects. common pattern: 50-75% overlap for passage-level tasks, then dedupe and use a recombine prompt that asks the model to merge overlapping outputs. For summarization across docs, we often produce chunk summaries then summarize summaries (hierarchical).
[08:56] Emily: how do you prevent drift when summarizing summaries? we worry about compounding errors.
[09:01] Priya: use retrieval-augmented grounding in the recombine step and keep links to source passages for verification; also keep an eval set. Redwood can surface token-level attributions to help debug regressions.
[09:15] Marcus: operational tip — stash a lightweight condensed context (dense-vector summary or smaller cache) to accelerate warm starts; that helps reduce recompute on cold sessions.
[09:28] Evan: we'd like to run a 128k benchmark using our data. what's the best way to do that?
[09:34] Alex: we'll send you the perf spreadsheet and a runbook. Priya can run an internal sim and then we can schedule a joint benchmark on Dedicated capacity with your sample docs and network topology. expect to measure throughput, 95/99 latencies, KV memory, and eviction behavior.
[09:50] Priya: for the joint run, please include: 1) sample docs, 2) expected concurrency patterns, 3) preferred model family (if any), and 4) SLO targets. we'll instrument with tracing and share traces.
[10:03] Emily: on compliance — do you provide audit logs for on-prem?
[10:08] Marcus: yes, Console exports and local audit logs are supported; for Private we can integrate with your SIEM. we also support SAML/SSO and SCIM for user management.
[10:20] Samir: network egress: prefer no egress. can we ensure control plane or telemetry doesn't leak data?
[10:27] Alex: with Private on-prem you can disable telemetry and keep control plane local. with VPC peering we also have options to limit egress. details will be in the VPC-onprem-checklist doc we'll share.
[10:40] [10:50] Evan: any gotchas when running FlashAttention with int8 quantized KV?
[10:54] Priya: mixing kernels is tricky — some FlashAttention kernels expect float16 intermediates; we use hybrid paths where KV is quantized on-disk but dequantized when used in compute, or we use int8-aware attention kernels where available. that tradeoff affects latency. we can show profiler traces.
[11:14] Emily: do you support partial attention recompute so we only re-evaluate cross-chunk attention for recent windows?
[11:20] Priya: yes, the runtime supports partial recompute and incremental attention, you can configure how many tokens to keep hot. it's a knob in the Dedicated config.
[11:32] Alex: let's surface some concrete next steps.
[11:36] Evan: yep.
[11:38] Alex: action items: we'll share the deck and spreadsheet; Priya will run internal sims and give preliminary numbers; customer to upload samples and IAM. we'll schedule the joint benchmark the week of 2026-03-09.
[11:50] Emily: sounds good. thanks.
[11:53] Evan: thanks everyone.

Recap / Notes (auto):
- Primary ask: evaluate 128k+ long-context serving with 95th latency target ~500ms and ~20 concurrent sessions.
- Options discussed: native 128k model vs chunk+recombine with KV cache.
- Key tradeoffs: KV memory (per-token), quantization effects on quality, batching vs tail latency, and attention kernel choices (FlashAttention, sparse/windowed).
- Ops: Dedicated/VPC recommended, pin kernels and use pinning for hot sessions, optional on-prem air-gapped deployment.
- Risks: quantization-induced regression, cache eviction tail latency, and model extrapolation limitations for positional encodings.

Links / artifacts to send: 128k-long-context-deep-dive deck (link), perf-benchmarks-128k.csv (link), VPC-onprem-checklist.docx (link), Redwood Optimize quant profiles doc (link).

End of transcript.
